SATOM 1.5.0

Thresholds you set once per product, building appliances from nothing on Proxmox VE or VMware ESXi, a trust store for your own CAs, and FortiAuthenticator as a fully managed product.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-08-06 · All releases

In short#

This is a large release with four main themes:

  • Thresholds per product. You can now set alert limits once for each product, mute a single probe for a limited time, and see the health of the SATOM machine itself.
  • Building appliances. SATOM can now create an appliance virtual machine from nothing on Proxmox VE or VMware ESXi.
  • Trust store. You can import your company's own certificate authorities, so certificate checking can stay on for privately signed devices.
  • FortiAuthenticator. It becomes a fully managed product, with its own Analysis page and Analytics boards.

The release also fixes many places where one ADOM showed another product's devices, data or pages.

What's new#

Monitoring and alerting#

Settings → Thresholds#

A new Thresholds tab in Settings lets you set a limit once instead of on every probe. There are six scopes: each of the four product ADOMs, SATOM itself, and the machine SATOM runs on.

  • If you leave a value empty on a probe, the probe inherits its product's value when it is graded.
  • 0 still means "switch this level off". An empty value and 0 are never treated the same.
  • Both probe pages show the number in use and where it comes from: set on this probe, inherited from the product, or factory default. That way you can always trace a grade back to the number behind it.

Severity for conditions with no number#

Some conditions have no number to compare: every backend of a policy is down, a policy is disabled by an administrator, the proxy daemon has stopped, or a monitored interface has changed. You can now raise, lower or silence each of these per product. A silenced condition is still shown on the probe. Silencing changes the grade, not what you see.

Mute one probe for a limited time#

You can mute a single probe for up to 720 hours, and you must give a reason.

  • The probe keeps running and keeps showing its own status.
  • It no longer raises the device badge or the alert mail.
  • Both the badge and the alert mail report it as lost coverage.
  • There is no permanent mute.

Health of the SATOM machine#

SATOM now checks its own machine's disk, memory and load on both HA nodes, and raises alerts about them. Before this release nothing measured the machine itself, so its disk could fill up while every indicator stayed green and no mail went out. A disk is graded critical at 92%. The limit is deliberately below 95%, because a full disk stops the database from writing.

Building appliances from nothing#

Settings → Hypervisors#

Register the Proxmox VE and VMware ESXi hosts SATOM may build machines on. You can register more than one of each.

  • Credentials are stored encrypted and are never sent back to your browser. If you leave the secret blank when editing a host, the stored secret is kept.
  • The Test button reports what the host will actually let SATOM do, including when its API is read-only. You find out about a limit here, not halfway through a build.
  • The tab also compares what the two hypervisor types can do and explains why.

Device Provisioning#

A new Device Provisioning page, available in every ADOM, builds an appliance virtual machine from nothing. It then hands the machine to System Provisioning for its configuration.

  • Five modes: Full, Semi, DHCP, VM only and Config only. The page lists the advantages and disadvantages of each.
  • Preflight first. Every mode is checked against the live hypervisor before anything changes.
  • Logged step by step. Each run records every step it takes. If a run fails partway, its rollback undoes only what that run created.
  • Addresses. An address SATOM took from IPAM can be given back. An address you typed yourself is never released.
  • Scoped to the ADOM. A run belongs to the ADOM it was started from, and other ADOMs cannot open it.

Proxmox VE and VMware ESXi#

  • Proxmox VE was tested end to end on a live host: create, power on, power off and delete.
  • VMware ESXi: reading from a standalone ESXi 8.0.3 host was tested live.
  • Free ESXi licence. With the free licence, the ESXi API is read-only. If you give SATOM the host's SSH credentials, it creates, powers on and off, and deletes machines through the host's own shell instead. If SSH is off, SATOM tells you how to turn it on, but it never turns it on itself.
  • Limits are reported, not assumed. SATOM reports what a host cannot do and why. A capability it cannot confirm is never treated as allowed.

Firmware library: install images and upgrade images#

Fortinet publishes two kinds of image for each release, and one cannot be used in place of the other. The firmware library now keeps them apart:

  • Each image is marked as an upgrade image or an install image. All existing images are upgrade images.
  • Install images are also marked for KVM or VMware.
  • The file types you can upload depend on the kind of image. Before this release the page could not hold install media at all.

Trust store for your own certificate authorities#

Before this release, a device with a privately signed certificate gave you two options. You could check it against the public certificate authorities, which it could never pass, or check nothing at all. As a result, a private fleet usually ran with certificate checking turned off.

Settings → Trust store fixes this:

  • Import your CAs. The tab has one slot for your Root CA and one for your Intermediate CA. You can paste the certificate or upload a file. Both are imported together, so a chain is never half-applied, and a whole chain pasted at once also works.
  • SATOM reads each certificate's role itself. A root pasted into the intermediate slot is still recorded as a root.
  • Device checks use both. SATOM checks devices against the public authorities plus your own.
  • Wrong certificates are refused at import. A certificate that is not a CA is rejected, with the reason. An incomplete chain is shown on the page, so you do not discover it at connection time.
  • Per-device test. A test for each device tells you which of three problems you have: an untrusted issuer, a hostname that does not match, or an expired certificate. Each needs a different fix.
  • Replicated and backed up. Your CAs are copied to the standby node and included in backups.

FortiAuthenticator becomes a managed product#

FortiAuthenticator is no longer a placeholder ADOM. It was tested against a FortiAuthenticator virtual machine running 8.0.3.

  • SATOM connects to the device's API. Its endpoint registry holds 40 endpoints, chosen from the 58 the unit advertises.
  • 28 section pages mirror the device's own menu.
  • API console. It does a dry run by default, records what you do in the audit log, and needs the matching permission.
  • Configuration harvest. The device's configuration is collected into the configuration source of truth and included in the fleet-wide scheduled sweeps.

Analysis for FortiAuthenticator#

An identity appliance has no traffic to chart, so its Analysis page answers the questions it does have:

  • Licence headroom. An unlicensed unit refuses the sixth user outright, and no CPU chart warns you of that.
  • Identity objects. Which identity objects exist on the unit.
  • Missing settings. Authentication settings whose absence is the finding.

The page also follows a few rules:

  • Not harvested is shown differently from 0, because each one calls for a different action.
  • The licence and token probes own the thresholds. A capacity row with no probe reads unmonitored, never ok.

Analytics boards for FortiAuthenticator#

Two new boards: fac-entitlement shows the licence and token figures, and fac-identity shows the same signals through their probes, with your thresholds.

Analysis for FortiADC#

The FortiADC ADOM now has its own Analysis page, built around the objects an ADC actually has:

  • virtual servers
  • pools and their members
  • real servers
  • health checks
  • the security profiles each virtual server uses
  • client SSL profiles
  • local certificates

On a real fleet the new page found problems the old page could not show, including a certificate 26 days from expiry and a pool sending traffic to a member with no health check.

User guide#

  • Five ADOMs. The manual now describes five ADOMs, not three. FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator have their own sections, including how to register them, and there is a table of what Analysis shows for each product.
  • New sections cover provisioning new appliances, updating SATOM itself, metrics collection, Analytics boards, period reports and the trust store.
  • Provisioning trade-offs. The provisioning section explains the choice, not just the steps: Proxmox VE against ESXi, the ESXi shell option and what it costs, the storage roles on Proxmox, the advantages and disadvantages of every mode, and where the management address comes from. Seven provisioning entries were added to Troubleshooting.

What changes for you#

  • Analysis moved into the Monitoring submenu. It used to be a separate item under Fleet. It now sits with the other Monitoring entries in every ADOM.
  • Device health limits are set per product. These include how old cached data may be, the critical multiplier, the run of failed harvests allowed, and the capacity levels. A FortiAnalyzer refreshes on a different rhythm than a FortiWeb, and one limit for both left correct devices permanently amber.
  • New probes inherit their limits. Discovery no longer writes fixed limits onto a new probe; the probe inherits them from its product. Existing probes that still had exactly the old default limits were switched to inheritance on first start, which changes nothing on the day. Probes with any other value were left alone.
  • Alert mails name the Thresholds scope that applies to each finding.
  • New appliance offers only the right platforms. A product ADOM now offers only its own platform, and Global offers all of them. FortiAuthenticator can now be added.
  • The firmware page is in every product ADOM and shows only that product's images.
  • Parked appliances are no longer probed on a schedule. Scheduled monitoring runs now skip appliances in maintenance. Probe now still reaches them. A probe that checks a plain address with no appliance behind it is never treated as parked.
  • FortiWeb-only boards stay in FortiWeb. The built-in Traffic and Service health boards now appear only in the FortiWeb ADOM.

Fixed#

One ADOM showing another product's data#

  • The FortiAuthenticator ADOM showed everything. It listed every appliance and every notification in the fleet, and the FortiAuthenticator appliance also appeared under FortiWeb. The same mistake affected alerts, the Certificate Manager, the plugin device picker and the Metrics change history, and Metrics showed FortiWeb totals under other ADOMs. Every product is now scoped correctly as soon as it is added, even if its ADOM is inactive.
  • The FortiADC and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs showed the FortiWeb WAF dashboard on Analysis, with every panel at zero. An empty panel looks "quiet", not "not applicable".
  • Reports for one product included another product's figures. A FortiAuthenticator report carried FortiWeb throughput. Reports now cover only their own product and leave out sections that do not apply, rather than showing zero.
  • The firmware page showed images from other products, and an upload could file an image under the wrong product. It was also unreachable from the FortiADC and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs.
  • Appliance detail, edit and delete could be opened from another ADOM by anyone who knew the device's number. They now follow the same rules as the appliance list. Global still reaches everything.
  • Adding a device could save it where you could not see it. From one ADOM you could pick another product's platform, and the saved device then did not appear, which looked like a failed save.
  • "New appliance" could not add a FortiAuthenticator, so its own ADOM had no way to add devices.
  • Device Provisioning behaved like a FortiWeb page. Opening it from Global showed only FortiWeb runs and no product picker.

Alerts and monitoring#

  • Healthy appliances were reported stale for 18 hours out of every 24. Every product other than FortiWeb reported "no cached configuration" while holding a snapshot minutes old.
  • False configuration-drift alerts. After the configuration source of truth moved out of git, drift detection reported the move as device-side edits. Retired appliances also kept raising drift alerts.
  • Alert mails ignored per-product capacity limits.
  • The transactions probe could have counted too little. On upgraded installations its lookback window could have shrunk from six hours to one, so a busy service would have looked quiet.
  • Missing threshold lines. Charts showed no threshold line for a probe that inherits its limits, even though it was graded against one.
  • Parked devices kept the monitoring check failing. The operator console's monitoring check counted the probes you disabled on a parked device as lost coverage, so it stayed at FAIL. A live probe at critical still fails the check.

FortiAuthenticator records failed to save#

FortiAuthenticator's internal product name is longer than any before it, and several places in the database could not store it. The first record saved for a FortiAuthenticator failed. Audit entries, device alerts and API tokens would have failed later, long after the device seemed fully set up. Existing installations are widened automatically at start-up. Nothing is ever shortened.

Provisioning#

  • Saving a hypervisor host failed the first time, every time. It also left an entry without credentials behind, which then failed its connection test with a misleading authentication error.
  • The storage for hypervisor hosts and provisioning runs was never created.
  • A wrong storage warning on Proxmox VE. The storage check told you to add a content type the host already had.
  • A newly created machine could be reported as missing. SATOM now asks the host directly instead of reading a list that refreshes only every so often.

Operator console#

  • The code-freshness check missed page-layout changes. The check that tells you whether each service runs the code on disk ignored changes to page layouts. After such a change without a restart, a page element could appear and vanish at random. The check now reports it and names what changed.
  • Hidden scratch and backup files no longer count as new code. They could send you to restart a service for nothing.

Under the hood#

  • The hypervisor support needs no extra software, so the offline install bundles did not have to grow.
  • The safeguards for ADOM scoping and for the two alert checks are now documented, and new products are covered automatically.
